questions.prompt: Why should apps store authentication tokens in the Keychain rather than in UserDefaults?

options.text: Keychain encrypts items with hardware-backed keys and protects secrets from unencrypted backups.
options.explanation: Keychain uses hardware encryption keys from the Secure Enclave to protect secrets.

options.text: UserDefaults limits saved strings to sixty-four characters and truncates long auth tokens.
options.explanation: UserDefaults has no string length limit and does not truncate strings.

options.text: iOS purges UserDefaults data automatically whenever the user closes the application.
options.explanation: UserDefaults data is persistent across app launches and remains on disk.

options.text: Keychain items compress stored data to take up zero bytes of local disk space on device.
options.explanation: Keychain items occupy database space and do not compress data to zero bytes.

questions.prompt: What happens to Keychain items when a user removes an app from their iPhone?

options.text: iOS deletes the Keychain items immediately when the app bundle is removed.
options.explanation: Keychain items are managed by securityd and are not deleted when an app is removed.

options.text: Keychain items stay stored on the device and remain available after a reinstall.
options.explanation: Keychain items persist across app uninstalls on the same physical hardware.

options.text: iOS moves the Keychain items into iCloud Drive inside a hidden public folder.
options.explanation: Keychain items are not moved to iCloud Drive when an app is deleted.

options.text: iOS converts Keychain items into temporary cache files in Library/Caches.
options.explanation: Keychain items remain in the encrypted system database, not in Library/Caches.

questions.prompt: Which Keychain item class is standard for storing application passwords and API tokens?

options.explanation: kSecClassCertificate stores X.509 public certificates rather than application tokens.
kSecClassIdentity binds a certificate to its private key rather than standard passwords.
kSecClassGenericPassword is the standard class for app passwords and auth tokens.
kSecClassKey stores cryptographic keys for encryption rather than generic passwords.

questions.prompt: How can an iOS app share Keychain credentials with its widget extension?

options.text: By storing credentials in the public Documents directory with shared read permissions.
options.explanation: Documents directory files are not automatically shared between separate sandbox containers.

options.text: By posting a Darwin notification containing the plaintext token in its payload string.
options.explanation: Darwin notifications cannot carry sensitive data payloads between extension processes.

options.text: By writing the secret into the global system clipboard with persistent pasteboard access.
options.explanation: The system pasteboard is insecure and accessible to third-party applications.

options.text: By configuring a shared Keychain Access Group entitlement across both app targets.
options.explanation: Keychain Access Groups let apps from the same development team share items.

questions.prompt: Which OSStatus constant indicates that a Keychain operation completed successfully?

options.explanation: errSecSuccess has an integer value of zero and signifies a successful call.
errSecItemNotFound indicates that the requested item does not exist in Keychain.
errSecDuplicateItem indicates that an item matching the query already exists.
errSecAuthFailed indicates that biometric or passcode authentication failed.

questions.prompt: What error status does SecItemAdd return when adding an item that already exists?

options.explanation: errSecItemNotFound is returned when reading or deleting a nonexistent item.
errSecDuplicateItem (-25299) indicates that the item already exists in Keychain.
errSecMissingEntitlement indicates missing capabilities rather than duplicate records.
errSecDecode indicates corrupted data rather than a duplicate entry.

questions.prompt: Which accessibility attribute enables a background fetch task to read an auth token while locked?

options.explanation: WhenUnlocked blocks access whenever the device display is locked by the user.
This policy requires an active passcode and blocks access while the screen is locked.
AfterFirstUnlock keeps items decrypted after the initial passcode entry post boot.
AccessibleAlways was deprecated due to severe security vulnerabilities when locked.

questions.prompt: Which system daemon manages the iOS Keychain database and coordinates access control?

options.explanation: launchd manages system processes and daemons rather than Keychain encryption.
cfprefsd manages UserDefaults property lists rather than Keychain storage.
containermanagerd manages app sandbox directories rather than Keychain database records.
securityd is the system daemon that manages Keychain databases and access control.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended practice when SecItemAdd returns errSecDuplicateItem?

options.text: Call SecItemUpdate to update attributes, or delete the old item and call SecItemAdd.
options.explanation: SecItemUpdate or deleting the existing entry resolves duplicate item collisions.

options.text: Force unwrap the return value and ignore the error code during app launch.
options.explanation: Ignoring duplicate item errors prevents new tokens from saving correctly.

options.text: Reboot the iOS device programmatically to clear the corrupted system database.
options.explanation: Apps cannot reboot iOS devices, and duplicate items are normal expected conditions.

options.text: Switch to storing the sensitive auth token in an unencrypted UserDefaults key.
options.explanation: UserDefaults is unencrypted and should never store sensitive authentication tokens.

questions.prompt: Why did Apple deprecate kSecAttrAccessibleAlways in iOS 9?

options.text: Because it caused excessive battery drain during background sync cycles.
options.explanation: Battery usage was not the reason for deprecating kSecAttrAccessibleAlways.

options.text: Because it left secret data accessible even while the device remained locked.
options.explanation: Leaving items decrypted while locked leaves secrets vulnerable to extraction.

options.text: Because it restricted Keychain items to a maximum payload size of eight bytes.
options.explanation: AccessibleAlways had no eight-byte payload size restriction.

options.text: Because it prevented apps from compiling with the modern Swift compiler.
options.explanation: The deprecation was driven by cryptographic security concerns, not compiler features.

questions.prompt: Where are hardware root encryption keys for Keychain data generated and protected?

options.text: Inside the Secure Enclave dedicated security coprocessor.
options.explanation: The Secure Enclave hardware handles root cryptographic keys isolated from the main CPU.

options.text: Inside the application sandbox preferences directory.
options.explanation: Application sandboxes cannot store hardware root keys securely.

options.text: Inside remote Apple CloudKit servers during initial device setup.
options.explanation: Device hardware root keys are generated on-device and never leave the Secure Enclave.

options.text: Inside the mobile baseband cellular modem firmware chip.
options.explanation: Cellular modems handle wireless transmission, not system cryptographic storage.

questions.prompt: Why should developers avoid storing large media files or databases directly in the Keychain?

options.text: Because Keychain automatically converts all media files into monochrome bitmaps.
options.explanation: Keychain stores raw bytes and does not alter image formats.

options.text: Because Keychain is optimized for small secrets and degrades performance with large blobs.
options.explanation: Keychain database operations slow down significantly when storing large multi-megabyte payloads.

options.text: Because the Security framework deletes any item larger than four kilobytes on boot.
options.explanation: Security framework does not automatically delete items based on size.

options.text: Because Apple App Store review automatically flags Keychain queries with media assets.
options.explanation: App Review does not inspect binary sizes of Keychain items directly.

questions.prompt: Compare UserDefaults and Keychain in iOS. In your answer, explain differences in encryption, typical use cases, and what happens to stored data when a user uninstalls the app.
questions.modelAnswer: UserDefaults stores unencrypted property lists on disk, suitable only for lightweight preferences like UI themes and onboarding flags. Its files are deleted when the user uninstalls the app. In contrast, Keychain provides hardware-backed AES-256 encryption via securityd and Secure Enclave. This makes it the proper place for passwords and auth tokens. Keychain items also persist on the device across app uninstalls.

rubric.criterion: Explains that UserDefaults stores plaintext unencrypted property lists while Keychain provides hardware-backed AES-256 encryption via the Secure Enclave.
Identifies appropriate use cases: UserDefaults for lightweight preferences and UI flags, and Keychain for secrets like auth tokens and passwords.
Clarifies lifecycle difference on uninstall: UserDefaults is deleted with the app sandbox, whereas Keychain items persist on the device.

questions.prompt: Explain the roles of SecItemAdd, SecItemCopyMatching, and SecItemDelete in Keychain Services. What common query keys are required to uniquely identify a generic password item?
questions.modelAnswer: SecItemAdd saves a new item into Keychain, returning errSecDuplicateItem if it already exists. SecItemCopyMatching searches for and retrieves matching attributes or decrypted data, returning errSecItemNotFound when missing. SecItemDelete removes items matching a query dictionary. To identify a generic password, set kSecClass to kSecClassGenericPassword. Also provide kSecAttrService for the service name and kSecAttrAccount for the user account.

rubric.criterion: Explains the CRUD functions: SecItemAdd saves new items, SecItemCopyMatching retrieves items, and SecItemDelete removes items matching queries.
Specifies kSecClass with kSecClassGenericPassword as the item category.
Names kSecAttrService and kSecAttrAccount as the primary keys that uniquely identify the stored password entry.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked and kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock. When would an iOS app require the AfterFirstUnlock attribute?
questions.modelAnswer: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked permits cryptographic access only while the device display is unlocked by the user. If the device locks, the item cannot be read. In contrast, kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock decrypts items after the user enters their passcode once following a device boot, and remains accessible even when the screen locks. Apps require AfterFirstUnlock for background tasks such as silent push notification handling or background fetch that need auth tokens.

rubric.criterion: Explains that WhenUnlocked only permits decryption when the device is currently unlocked by the user.
Explains that AfterFirstUnlock allows decryption once the user has unlocked the device after a reboot, even if the screen is currently locked.
Explains the scenario requiring AfterFirstUnlock: background tasks such as background fetch, silent push notifications, or background audio.

questions.prompt: How can an iOS app share an authentication token with its Widget extension? Describe the necessary Xcode entitlement and the Keychain query attribute used.
questions.modelAnswer: To share a Keychain item, enable the Keychain Sharing capability in both targets. Configure the exact same Keychain Access Group for each target. The group identifier must use the shared Apple Developer Team ID prefix. When saving or reading the token, the app includes kSecAttrAccessGroup in the query dictionary set to that shared group name.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the need to enable the Keychain Sharing capability and configure a shared Keychain Access Group in both targets.
Mentions that both targets must share the same Apple Developer Team ID prefix for access group entitlement verification.
Specifies passing kSecAttrAccessGroup with the shared group name in the Keychain query dictionary.

questions.prompt: Why can Keychain items from a previous install cause unexpected bugs on a fresh app installation, and how should an app handle this situation?
questions.modelAnswer: Keychain items persist across app uninstalls. If a user deletes and reinstalls the app, old auth tokens may still exist. This can cause the app to assume the user is logged in. To handle this, store a boolean flag in UserDefaults such as hasLaunchedBefore. Because UserDefaults is wiped on deletion, a missing flag indicates a fresh install. The app can then delete stale Keychain items before proceeding.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Keychain items persist across app uninstallation, leaving stale auth tokens or user IDs when an app is reinstalled.
Describes using a first-launch flag in UserDefaults to detect a clean installation.
Explains clearing stale Keychain items upon detecting a first launch to establish a clean state.

questions.prompt: Write a Swift function keychainStatusMessage(status:) taking an OSStatus code. Return 'Success', 'Duplicate item', 'Item not found', or 'Unhandled error' based on the status.
questions.modelAnswer:
import Foundation
import Security

func keychainStatusMessage(status: OSStatus) -> String {
    switch status {
    case errSecSuccess:
        return "Success"
    case errSecDuplicateItem:
        return "Duplicate item"
    case errSecItemNotFound:
        return "Item not found"
    default:
        return "Unhandled error"
    }
}

print(keychainStatusMessage(status: errSecSuccess))
print(keychainStatusMessage(status: errSecDuplicateItem))
print(keychainStatusMessage(status: errSecItemNotFound))

verify.output:
Success
Duplicate item
Item not found

rubric.criterion: Handles errSecSuccess by returning 'Success'.
Handles errSecDuplicateItem and errSecItemNotFound with their respective strings.
Provides a default fallback that returns 'Unhandled error'.

questions.prompt: Write a Swift function makeReadTokenQuery(service:account:) that constructs a Keychain query dictionary for reading a single token. The query must specify kSecClassGenericPassword, service, account, kSecReturnData as true, and kSecMatchLimit as kSecMatchLimitOne.
questions.modelAnswer:
import Foundation
import Security

func makeReadTokenQuery(service: String, account: String) -> [String: Any] {
    return [
        kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
        kSecAttrService as String: service,
        kSecAttrAccount as String: account,
        kSecReturnData as String: true,
        kSecMatchLimit as String: kSecMatchLimitOne
    ]
}

let q = makeReadTokenQuery(service: "authService", account: "userA")
let returnsData = (q[kSecReturnData as String] as? Bool) == true
print("Returns data: \(returnsData)")

rubric.criterion: Sets kSecClass to kSecClassGenericPassword.
Assigns service and account to kSecAttrService and kSecAttrAccount.
Sets kSecReturnData to true to request raw data return.
Sets kSecMatchLimit to kSecMatchLimitOne.
